title: India's Gen Z Storms the Streets but Remains Invisible in Parliament
excerpt: The 'Cockroach' protest movement forced a cabinet minister's resignation, yet Indians under 35 hold barely any seats in the legislatures that govern them.
body:
• The Cockroach Janta Party movement forced Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation — a rare retreat for Modi's government
  • Indians under 30 are three times as likely as the average citizen to be unemployed, yet youth representation in Parliament and state assemblies remains negligible
  • At least two dozen public exams have been invalidated due to leaks since 2014, fuelling a systemic crisis of trust in India's examination system

A Movement Named After an Insult

When India's chief justice earlier this year made a disparaging remark about unemployed youth, the young people he dismissed turned the slur into a rallying cry. The Cockroach Janta Party — a satirical "people's party" — erupted after the government invalidated national medical exam results for roughly two million students following the discovery that test questions had been leaked.

On July 20, more than 50,000 protesters attempted to march on Parliament, according to some estimates. Police responded with force, but the crackdown only widened sympathy. Bollywood stars voiced support on social media. The crowds, which by then spanned age groups and socioeconomic classes, swelled across cities.

"People are usually divided by religion, caste and language. This was the first time they united around education."

— Ashok Kumar, 25-year-old protester from Bihar

By the end of the week, the movement had its scalp: Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned — a rare concession from a government that has seldom yielded to street pressure. Prime Minister Modi also announced a panel to review the examination system and agreed to compensate families of students who died by suicide after exam papers were leaked.

Loud on the Streets, Missing from the House

The paradox at the heart of India's youth politics is stark. Some 900 million Indians are under the age of 35, making it one of the youngest major democracies on earth. Yet their representation in Parliament and state assemblies remains negligible. The average age of a Lok Sabha MP hovers well above 50, and young candidates struggle to secure party tickets in a political culture that rewards seniority and dynastic ties over generational change.

The gap is not for lack of political energy. India's Gen Z has proven adept at organizing through social media, building coalitions that transcend the traditional fault lines of religion, caste, and language. But converting that street power into legislative seats requires navigating party structures dominated by older politicians with deep pockets and established patronage networks.

A Broken Ladder

The crisis that ignited the Cockroach movement runs deeper than any single exam leak. In India, standardized tests serve as the primary pathway to the middle class, rationing access to thousands of public-sector jobs — diplomats, administrators, clerks, and forest rangers — through gruelling examinations for which students spend years and small fortunes preparing. Success can be statistically harder than gaining admission to Harvard, according to Reuters, but the prize includes lifelong security, pensions, and housing benefits unavailable in the private sector.

Since 2014, at least two dozen exams have had their results invalidated due to leaks, according to a Reuters review of public records and media reports. Corporate job growth, meanwhile, has slowed to 3% annually from 11% in the decade before 2020, according to Marcellus Investment Managers.

"The public examination system has largely collapsed."

— Ashok Kumar, who has taken seven competitive exams in four years without clearing any

A Government Forced to Bend

The concessions marked a significant departure from the Modi government's usual playbook. "Modi's usual playbook of staying above the fray, making broad promises and shifting responsibility down the chain failed this time," political scientist Gilles Verniers of Sciences Po told Deutsche Welle. "The minister's resignation is a clear victory for the protesters and a personal setback for a prime minister who stood by him until the end."

The closest precedent was the farmers' protests of 2020-2021, during which an estimated 700 to 750 protesters died before the government repealed three contentious farm laws. But even then, legislation was withdrawn without ministerial accountability. This time, a cabinet minister paid a political price.

The Cockroach Janta Party has since called off further protests "in good faith" but warned it would return to the streets if promised reforms fail to materialize. Talks continue over a five-point charter for examination reform.

What Comes Next

The movement's lasting impact depends on whether street momentum can translate into structural change — both in examination governance and in youth political representation. The opposition Congress party called Pradhan's resignation "a victory for a generation tired of struggling in an unfair and corrupt system."

For the diaspora, the story resonates painfully. Many overseas Indians left precisely because merit-based pathways at home felt blocked. The spectacle of millions of young Indians spending years in cramming centres, only to have their results voided by systemic corruption, underscores the fragility of the social contract that India's growth story is built on.

As activist Amrita Johri told DW: "It shifted the debate from examination scandals to larger questions about whether India's institutions are still seen as fair, transparent and accountable."
